c: Greenfield Veterinary Clinic, a clinic with five veterinarians and 12 staff
s: Greenfield Veterinary Clinic uses paper charts and a simple spreadsheet for appointments. Appointments are double-booked weekly, records are hard to find and reminders are sent by hand. The practice manager wants to replace this process with a system and has a budget of $18,000.

The practice manager (judge) wants you to analyze the current system, identify the requirements and recommend a solution: buy a vet clinic management package, build a custom database, or use general-purpose cloud tools.
You have 7 minutes to present your analysis, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and recommend a design.
f: Staff: 5 veterinarians, 7 technicians and front-desk staff
Problems: double-booked appointments each week; missing records; manual reminders cost about 6 staff hours a week
Packaged vet software: $11,500 setup plus $240 a month
Custom database: about $16,000 to build plus maintenance
Cloud scheduling and records tools: about $4,200 a year but limited vet-specific features
d: present your systems analysis and recommendation
n: Describes the current system's problems and the requirements for a new one
Compares packaged software, a custom build and cloud tools on cost, fit and risk
Explains data needs, such as patient records, appointments and reminders, and privacy
Recommends an option and a phased implementation plan
Includes training, data migration and testing steps
Defines success measures such as no double bookings and hours saved
q: Why not just keep the spreadsheet and fix the double bookings?
What can go wrong when we move our paper records?
How would you train a staff who are afraid of new software?

c: Brightfield School District, a district with 8 schools and 5,200 students
s: Brightfield wants to launch a new student information portal before the new school year begins in 14 weeks. The project is behind schedule: requirements are still changing, the vendor delivered a late prototype, and the team has only two developers and a part-time tester. The district has $75,000 for the project, and $52,000 is already spent.

The technology director (judge) wants you to assess the project, compare options such as cutting features, adding staff, extending the schedule, or splitting the launch into phases, and recommend a plan.
You have 7 minutes to present your recommendation and explain the risks.
f: Budget: $75,000 total; $52,000 spent; 14 weeks remain
Features requested: attendance, grades, parent messaging, schedules, online forms
Tester available: 20 hours a week; the vendor prototype is two weeks late
Option: add a contract developer at $4,500 a month
Option: launch attendance and grades first, other features in January
n: Applies project management ideas: scope, schedule, budget and risk
Compares four options with pros and cons
Calculates what each option costs against the remaining $23,000
Recommends a phased launch with a tight scope for the first release
Addresses testing, security and student data privacy before launch
Defines milestones and a communication plan with schools and parents
q: What do you say to the principals who want every feature at launch?
How do you keep scope from growing again?
How would you decide that the first release is ready?

c: Peak Performance Sports Store, a retail chain with 9 locations
s: Peak Performance Sports Store tracks sales in separate systems at each location. Reports arrive late, and product names and codes differ across stores. Last season, two stores ran out of a top-selling shoe while another had 800 unsold pairs. The chief operating officer wants one reliable view of sales and inventory.

The COO (judge) wants you to explain how better data management would help, compare options such as a central database, a cloud inventory tool, or a manual reconciliation process, and recommend a plan.
You have 7 minutes to present your analysis and recommendation.
f: 9 stores with separate point-of-sale systems
Inventory mismatch last season: 800 unsold pairs of one shoe and stock-outs at two stores
Estimated lost sales and markdown cost: about $54,000
Central database project: $38,000 and 4 months; cloud inventory tool: $1,400 a month; manual reconciliation: one analyst, about $52,000 a year
Data issues: product codes differ in 3 of the 9 stores
n: Explains data quality, standard formats and a single source of truth
Compares a central database, a cloud tool and manual work, with costs and risks
Calculates cost over a year (cloud about $16,800, database about $38,000 once, manual about $52,000)
Recommends an approach and a phased rollout beginning with product codes
Covers data security, backups and access control
Defines measures such as stock-outs and markdown dollars
q: Why not just hire an analyst to fix the spreadsheets?
What is the first thing you would clean up?
How will we know the new data is accurate?

c: Meridian Law Group, a law firm with 24 employees
s: Meridian Law Group stores client files on a single office server that is eight years old. Last month the server crashed for two days, and the last full backup was three weeks old. Several attorneys lost work. The managing partner wants a plan to protect client data and keep the firm running.

The managing partner (judge) can invest up to $30,000. The options are a new on-site server with backups, moving to cloud storage, or a hybrid approach. Client confidentiality and ethics rules also apply.
You have 7 minutes to present your analysis, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and make a recommendation.
f: Current server: 8 years old; crash caused 2 days of downtime
Last full backup: three weeks old
New server and backup system: about $24,000 up front, $3,000 a year support
Cloud storage and services: about $1,100 a month
Hybrid: smaller server plus cloud backup, about $15,000 up front and $500 a month
n: Identifies risks: aging hardware, single point of failure, weak backups
Compares on-site, cloud and hybrid solutions with costs over 3 years
Covers security, encryption and compliance with client confidentiality
Recommends a plan with backups tested regularly
Includes a disaster recovery plan with recovery time goals
Describes migration steps with minimal downtime
q: How quickly could we be back up if something fails again?
Is it safe to put privileged client files in the cloud?
What happens if our internet goes down?

c: Fresh Basket Grocers, a chain of four grocery stores
s: Fresh Basket Grocers has heard about using artificial intelligence to predict demand and reduce food waste. The owner throws away about 9 percent of fresh produce each week, worth roughly $6,800 a month. A vendor pitches an AI forecasting tool for $14,000 a year. The staff are not experienced with it.
The owner (judge) wants to know whether the technology is a good investment, what the risks are, and what other approaches could reduce waste.
You have 7 minutes to explain how the technology works, compare it with alternatives and pros and cons, and recommend what to do.
f: Produce waste: about $6,800 per month
AI forecasting tool: $14,000 per year; the vendor claims a 30% reduction in waste
Alternative: better manual ordering using last year's sales, no added cost, estimated 10% reduction
Alternative: partnering with a food bank and marking down near-expiry items; $1,200 a year in labor
Data available: two years of point-of-sale data from all four stores
n: Explains in plain language how predictive analytics uses past sales data
Calculates the potential savings (30% is about $24,500 a year against the $14,000 cost)
Compares the AI tool, manual ordering and markdown or donation programs
Notes risks: data quality, vendor claims, staff training and privacy
Recommends a stepwise approach such as a pilot at one store
Defines measures for success
q: Do we have enough data for this to work?
What if the vendor's 30 percent doesn't happen?
Can we try it at one store first?
